lesson.title: Default Parameters: Giving Functions a Fallback Plan
lesson.summary: A default parameter value lets a function be called with fewer arguments than it defines, because Python fills in a preset value for any parameter the caller leaves out.
lesson.body:
Parameters describe what values a function needs from its caller, but not every call site wants to specify every single one. Default parameters solve this by letting a function's definition supply a fallback value for a parameter, which Python uses automatically whenever that argument is omitted from a call. This keeps the common case short while still allowing full customization when it is needed.

The syntax attaches an = and a value directly in the def line. Consider def greet(name, greeting="Hello"): print(f"{greeting}, {name}!"). Calling greet("Ana") supplies only name, so Python uses the default for greeting, printing "Hello, Ana!". Calling greet("Ana", "Hi") overrides the default, printing "Hi, Ana!" instead. The default is not a limit, it is only used when nothing else is provided for that spot.

One rule governs where defaults can appear: once a parameter in the def line has a default, every parameter after it must also have one, because Python matches leftover positional arguments to parameters in order and cannot skip over a required parameter that comes after an optional one. def greet(greeting="Hello", name): would raise a SyntaxError, since name has no default but follows one that does.

Default parameters also make it safe to grow a function's capabilities over time. Suppose greet was originally written as def greet(name): and later needed an optional greeting phrase. Adding it as greeting="Hello" instead of a required parameter means every existing call to greet("Ana") still works exactly as before, since the new parameter fills itself in automatically. A required parameter, by contrast, would break every one of those old calls until each was rewritten to supply it.

Default parameters carry a well-known trap when the default is a mutable object like a list or dictionary. The default value is created exactly once, at the moment the def statement runs, not fresh on every call. So a function like this behaves unexpectedly:

def add_item(item, cart=[]):
    cart.append(item)
    return cart

print(add_item("apple"))
print(add_item("banana"))

The first call appends "apple" to the default list and returns ['apple']. The second call does not get a fresh empty list; it reuses the same list object created back when the function was defined, so it appends "banana" onto the list that already holds 'apple', printing ['apple', 'banana']. The fix is to default to None instead, and build the real list inside the function body: def add_item(item, cart=None): if cart is None: cart = []; then append and return. Since a brand-new list is created inside the function on every call where cart was omitted, each call starts clean. This is exactly why None, covered as its own value in the previous chapter, is the standard sentinel for "no mutable default was given".
